extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, agents, applicants and IP practitioners interested in EPO practice
extracted.subtask_description: A summary of the principal updates to the European Patent Office Guidelines for Examination coming into force 1 March 2024, focusing on priority entitlement, inventive step/evidence, AI disclosure, sequence listings, antibodies, description adaptation, opposition acceleration and related examination practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to priority (A-III-6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent any substantiated indication to the contrary, there is a strong rebuttable presumption under the EPC that an applicant or joint applicants claiming priority in accordance with Art. 88(1) and Rule 52 are also entitled to the claimed priority. The burden of proof is shifted to the party challenging entitlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote from Guidelines: "Especially where an international application under the PCT is filed by joint applicants, including the priority applicant, but without naming the priority applicant as applicant for the European designation, the mere fact of the joint filing implies an agreement between the applicants allowing all of them to rely on the priority right, unless substantial facts indicate otherwise (see G 1/22 and G 2/22)". Practical implication: challengers (examining division, opponents, third parties) must prove lack of entitlement. The update follows EBA decisions G 1/22 and G 2/22 and could affect long-standing disputes over priority (e.g., CRISPR family).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step — reliance on technical effects (G2/21)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may rely upon a technical effect for inventive step if the skilled person, having the common general knowledge in mind, and based on the application as originally filed, would derive said effect as being encompassed by the technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Headnote II of G2/21. The Guidelines have been updated (G-VII-5.2,11) to reflect this but provide no further interpretative guidance. Boards of Appeal decisions have begun to clarify what it means for an effect to be "encompassed and embodied". Practically, the technical effect must be derivable from the original disclosure such that it is part of the same invention; mere post-filed assertions of effect are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free evaluation of evidence (E-IV-4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of free evaluation of evidence as articulated in G2/21 has been incorporated in the Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBA's decision on free evaluation of evidence is included in an update to E-IV-4.1. This reinforces that the assessment of evidence (e.g., experimental data, alleged technical effects) is for the deciding body to weigh; the Guidelines reflect that evidence must be considered in light of the application and common general knowledge. No detailed new criteria for weighing evidence were provided beyond incorporation of the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirements for AI-related inventions (F-III-3; G-II-3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI inventions require supporting data and examples similar to biotech: mathematical methods and training datasets must be disclosed in sufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed; otherwise the disclosure may amount to an invitation to a research programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines quote: "Occasionally applications are filed in which there is a fundamental insufficiency... another example can be found in the field of artificial intelligence if the mathematical methods and the training datasets are disclosed in insufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed. Such a lack of detail may result in a disclosure that is more like an invitation to a research programme" (F-III-3). Also: "The technical effect that a machine learning algorithm achieves may be readily apparent or established by explanations, mathematical proof, experimental data or the like. While mere allegations are not enough, comprehensive proof is not required, either. If the technical effect is dependent on particular characteristics of the training dataset used, those characteristics that are required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden using common general knowledge. However, in general, there is no need to disclose the specific training dataset itself" (G-II-3.3.1). Practical takeaways: provide sufficient methodological detail and dataset-relevant characteristics; allegations alone insufficient; full dataset usually not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: ST.26 sequence listings and divisional applications (A-IV-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: ST.26 standard applies to all new European applications filed after July 2022, including divisionals; applicants must convert ST.25 listings from a parent into ST.26 for new divisionals, but conversion risks adding matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical workaround quoted: add the ST.25 sequence listing to the end of the description of the divisional and file the ST.26 after the initial filing date. Risk: applicants may incur high excess page fees if listing is long. Guideline update provides an exception/fee waiver: "By way of exception, an additional fee is not due either for a parent application's ST.25 sequence listing filed in PDF format as part of a divisional application" (A-IV-5). Note also recognition that conversion from ST.25 to ST.26 can potentially add matter (as acknowledged by WIPO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of inventor must be a natural person (A-III-7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO will check that the designated inventor is a natural person; AI cannot be designated as an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update follows decision J 8/20 (DABUS). Practical consequence: applications designating non‑human inventors will be challenged; applicants should ensure inventor designation names natural persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration of opposition proceedings where UPC or national infringement actions pending (D-VIII-1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositions are to be given priority (accelerated processing) if a party has submitted a reasoned request for acceleration in a case where an infringement action in respect of the European patent is pending before the Unified Patent Court or a national court, or if the EPO is informed that infringement actions are pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines quote: "oppositions are to be given priority [...] if a party to the proceedings has submitted a reasoned request for accelerated processing in a case where an infringement action in respect of the European patent is pending before the Unified Patent Court or a national court of a contracting state, or if the EPO is informed by the Unified Patent Court, a national court or competent authority of a contracting state that infringement actions are pending" (D-VIII-1.2). Practically, parties with parallel infringement litigation can request prioritisation of opposition proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibodies — claiming genus by antigen/epitope; sufficiency and burden of proof (G-II-6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the EPO it is possible to claim a genus of antibodies according to their target antigen or epitope; the Guidelines clarify conditions when such claims are permitted, including sufficiency requirements and the burden of proof with respect to prior art antibodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updates reflect Boards of Appeal case law. The Guidelines provide further clarification on sufficiency and on who bears the burden to show lack of novelty/obviousness based on prior-art antibodies. Note that specific guidance relating to defining antibodies by epitope has been removed (i.e., less prescriptive guidance on epitope-based definitions). Practitioners should ensure sufficiency across claimed genus and be prepared to address prior‑art antibody comparisons and proof burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of the description when claims are amended (D-V-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of the patent may be examined for compliance with Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84; inconsistencies between description and claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote from Guidelines: "the description of the patent may be examined for compliance with the requirements of Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84. In particular, inconsistencies between the description and the claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject‑matter for which protection is sought must be avoided" (D‑V‑5). Context: controversy exists over requiring applicants to amend descriptions to align with allowed claims; a referral on the legality of forcing such amendments is pending. Practically, when claims are amended during opposition applicants should check and, where necessary, adapt the description to avoid inconsistencies that cause doubt about the scope.
